title: The Flagpole Faint
twist: Everyone assumes the hour of marching wore him out. The opposite is true: marching kept his leg muscles pumping blood back up, and standing perfectly still was the hard part.
briefing: Kofi, 15, marched and played the drum with the school band for an hour on a cool morning without any trouble. Then the band stood at attention, knees locked, for a 40-minute flag ceremony. Near the end he felt light-headed and his vision went grey at the edges.
question: Why was standing still harder on Kofi's body than marching?

clues.title: Fine while marching
clues.text: He marched and drummed for a full hour earlier with no problems at all. It was a cool, cloudy morning.
clues.shows: moving his legs keeping him fine for much longer

clues.title: Grey vision after 30 still minutes
clues.text: After about thirty minutes standing perfectly still, he felt woozy and his vision greyed at the edges.
clues.shows: less blood reaching his brain while he stood still

clues.title: Heavy, puffy legs
clues.text: His socks left deep marks around his ankles and his legs felt heavy and full.
clues.shows: blood and fluid collecting low in his legs

clues.title: Sitting fixed it fast
clues.text: He sat down with his head low and felt normal within a minute. The band director told everyone else to wiggle their toes and bend their knees.
clues.shows: helping blood get back to the heart fixing it quickly

hypotheses.text: He was worn out from the hour of marching earlier.
hypotheses.flaw: If marching had worn him out he'd have struggled while marching — instead he was fine until he stood still, and a minute's sit-down fixed it.
It was a cool, cloudy morning, and overheating doesn't explain heavy, puffy legs or why bending your knees helps.

hypotheses.text: He was nervous about the ceremony.
hypotheses.flaw: Nerves don't make ankles puffy, and they aren't fixed by wiggling your toes.

hypotheses.text: Standing still lets gravity pool blood in his legs; without leg muscles squeezing the veins, less blood gets back to his heart and up to his brain. Marching works those muscles, so it's easier.

transfer.context: Ana, 16, volunteers at a museum ticket desk, standing still for hours. By evening her ankles are puffy and she feels woozy — but on days she walks the galleries as a guide, she feels fine.
options: Standing still lets blood pool in her legs; walking makes her leg muscles pump it back up.
She is bored with the job.
transfer.retryHint: Kofi was fine during one activity and not the other — which clue showed that?
transfer.explanation: Same building, same air — the difference is whether her legs are moving. Walking squeezes her leg veins and pushes blood back up; standing still at the desk lets it pool, just as it did for Kofi at the flagpole.

takeaway: Your leg muscles help your veins. Moving squeezes blood back up to the heart; standing perfectly still lets it pool — so marching is easier on your brain than standing at attention.
